canberra.title: Mint channels 70 years of Australian television history
canberra.snippet: The Royal Australian Mint has unveiled a new exhibition and coin to honour 70 years of Australian television, with veteran broadcaster Pe...
canberra.content:
21 November 2026

Start the conversation

TV presenter Peter Overton and Royal Australian Mint CEO Emily Martin launch the new 70th Anniversary of Australian Television pop-up exhibition. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

The Royal Australian Mint has unveiled a new exhibition and coin to honour 70 years of Australian television, with veteran broadcaster Peter Overton officially launching the display.

The new exhibition features items from the archives of Channel 9, the network that delivered Australia’s first TV broadcast on 17 September 1956.

Included are the master tapes for the pilots of Skippy the Bush Kangaroo and McLeod’s Daughters, as well as film cameras used across the last 70 years and footage of some of the biggest news stories in Australian history.

A new 50-cent piece features streaks of colour with a traditional TV set pressed into the middle.

Channel 9 presenter and former 60 Minutes reporter Peter Overton joined Royal Australian Mint CEO Emily Martin to unveil the new exhibition.

Mr Overton said it was an honour to be invited to the Mint, confessing he is proud to be part of Australia’s broadcasting legacy.

“It’s so cool. I’ve been at Nine for 35 years, more than half my life, and I’ve seen great change in broadcasting. For the Mint to wrap their arms around it and say it’s an important part of our country, I think all of us across the industry are quite pleased,” he said.

“It’s been 70 years; we’ve had a lot of change, but we are still here. I think that means we’re doing something right.

“The future of TV might not be the same as it was in the past 70 years, but whether it be on phones or social media, it still plays a big part in people’s lives and connects people.”

70 Years of Australian TV Broadcasting commemorative coin. Photos: Royal Australian Mint.

Equipment from the Channel 9 archives.

TV sets from the last 70 years.

Exhibition curator Stephanie McCarthy-Reece said it was a surreal experience to work with pieces from the Channel 9 archive.

“To have Peter open something I’ve worked on is absolutely awesome; it’s not something I thought I’d ever get to do, but it was a real privilege,” she said.

“This has been about a two-month-long collaboration to get to this point.

“We’ve got truly historic Australian artifacts on display, as well as some of the amazing coins we have made along the way.

“I personally love the Neighbours coin because I think most people don’t know that we celebrate things like Neighbours and Home and Away, which many households have and still watch consistently.

“We wanted the exhibition to showcase things from several generations, so we’ve included coins from other broadcasting milestones as well, like 90 years of the ABC.”

Royal Australian Mint CEO Emily Martin said the commemorative coin offered Australians a chance to celebrate the television memories that have become part of their own stories.

“The coin captures the colour, character and nostalgia of Australian television. It’s a wonderful way to mark this milestone and celebrate the moments that have become part of our shared history,” Ms Martin said.

“Whether you grew up with black-and-white television or have watched the industry evolve through colour and digital broadcasting, the display is a celebration of the stories that have shaped how Australians see themselves and the world around them.”

The coin is available in a presentation card, with a 50c Coloured Silver Proof Coin also available in a storage case with a certificate of authenticity.

The commemorative coin can be purchased at the Royal Australian Mint or partner distributors for $30. A total of 50,000 will be pressed but will not be in general circulation.

canberra.title: MyWay+ still not up to scratch with contractor’s assurances ‘not proven reliable’
canberra.snippet: The Transport Minister cannot say when Canberra’s MyWay+ system will be fully rolled out as a “baseline” of what consti...
canberra.content:
21 November 2026

Start the conversation

MyWay+ is the project that keeps on delivering issues for the ACT Government. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The Transport Minister cannot say when Canberra’s MyWay+ system will be fully rolled out as a “baseline” of what constitutes a completed contract still hasn’t been established.

It’s almost two years since the beleaguered public transport system was launched, but milestones 29 and 30 remain outstanding.

Both were meant to be completed mid-last year.

Transport Minister Tara Cheyne said contractor NEC hasn’t been paid for those milestones because key system issues are unresolved, and there was no agreed understanding of what needed to be done to satisfy tender and contract completion conditions.

“What the last few months have been focused on is coming to an agreed position on exactly what is still outstanding,” she said.

“The overall system has not been fixed to a standard – or the evidence provided to the standard that we need – that it is fixed.”

Digital Canberra Chief Information Officer Veronica Morados stated this meant no completion date could be determined.

“There’s still some ongoing negotiations in relation to those two remaining milestones,” she said.

“However, work is continuing with NEC for some of the remaining, or outstanding, issues that we have.”

One of those issues is with the reliability of fare-enforcement devices.

Ms Morados said there were a “family of issues” causing the machines to fail, and the root cause still hadn’t been fully identified.

“Instead of just accepting that a particular symptom has been fixed, we want to make sure that the root cause has been addressed,” she said.

Ms Cheyne explained further that NEC had said the devices were “good to go”, but in practice they weren’t.

“Too often, NEC has provided us with assurances that have not proved reliable on the ground,” she said.

Other issues that also need to be addressed include allowing passengers to use the Apple Express Transit mode to pay fares, and enabling MyWay+ family accounts.

No timeframes could be provided on when those features will be made available.

But passenger information displays are likely to take much longer to become reality.

Ms Cheyne said it was a capability she was “super keen” for Canberrans to access, but the MyWay+ contract and funding didn’t include that type of infrastructure.

Thus, it will need additional funding.

“I’m trying to figure out how to get that done,” Ms Cheyne said.

It’s left the ACT Greens wondering why the government kept working with NEC to deliver the contract’s final milestones.

“NEC continues to take Canberra for a ride,” ACT Greens transport spokesperson Andrew Braddock said.

“This is the latest event in a saga plagued by delays and bereft of accountability.”

“How many times must NEC assure the government that something works before it actually does?”

Mr Braddock questioned why other jurisdictions were able to deliver improvements on their ticketing systems while the ACT continued to argue with its contractor about whether the equipment actually worked.

“It’s extraordinary that the minister herself has had to lay bare the failures of the government’s own contractor, despite NEC’s repeated promises that the problems had been fixed,” he said.

“How many more failures, how many more excuses, and how much more taxpayer money will it take before the government admits that the real question isn’t when MyWay+ will be fixed but whether it was worth the investment?”

canberra.title: By day he’s Santa. At home, Dallas is caring for the love of his life
canberra.snippet: As his wife Bonnie sleeps, Dallas Atkins cleans their apartment well into the night. When Bonnie emerges in the morning to find everythin...
canberra.content:
Dallas and his wife Bonnie, who is living with Alzheimer’s disease. The couple will celebrate 40 years of marriage in 2027. Photo: Supplied.

As his wife Bonnie sleeps, Dallas Atkins cleans their apartment well into the night.

When Bonnie emerges in the morning to find everything tidied away, she asks with wonder whether Santa and his elves have been busy. Dallas plays along, assuring her the elves have indeed been helping with the housework.

It’s a sweet exchange, but there’s more to the story.

Bonnie, whose full name is Bronwyn, is living with Alzheimer’s disease, and her husband of almost 40 years just happens to be one of Canberra’s best-known shopping mall Santas.

But Dallas is no ordinary Santa. His jovial personality is a perfect blend of Kurt Russell’s charm, Tim Allen’s comedy and a little of St Nick’s magic. It’s a personality shaped by decades as a musician, magician and children’s entertainer, with a stint as an Army musician thrown into the mix.

Santa Dallas brings a little Christmas magic to Westfield Woden. Photo: Supplied.

After five years in the red suit, Dallas has become a Santa ambassador and a trainer for Scene to Believe, the company behind Christmas photography experiences at shopping centres across Australia. He’s the Santa at Westfield Woden this year.

Dallas reckons “going the extra mile” to create lasting memories is what keeps families coming back year after year. But as I chat to him, I realise he’s exactly what a true Santa should be: theatrical and authentic.

He’s all about putting on a show. As we’re chatting, he jumps from his chair to demonstrate his signature ‘invisible ball’ trick. And when it comes to authenticity, even his beard gets the full treatment; a stubborn dark patch is bleached white each Christmas. (He also lets slip that Santas with real beards earn a little extra.)

“If I’m going to do it, I’ll do it right,” Dallas says.

Long before he bleached his beard, Dallas was organising music events at Canberra’s Albert Hall in the mid-1980s, bringing together local bands, including, as fate would have it, a young musician named Bonnie.

She was performing with a group called Faith, and the pair went on to build a colourful life together, filled with music, travel, raising two sons and running an antique shop on Crookwell’s main street.

Dallas and Bonnie on their wedding day in 1987. The couple celebrate 40 years together next year. Photo: Supplied

But in recent years, their lives have taken an unexpected turn.

After returning to Canberra from Crookwell in 2021, Bonnie’s memory difficulties became increasingly apparent. One morning, she became lost on her way to work after getting off the bus at the wrong stop. Her employer also noticed she was struggling with tasks that had once been second nature.

Earlier symptoms had initially been attributed to menopause, but further investigations eventually revealed Alzheimer’s disease. By the time she was diagnosed, Dallas says the disease was already advanced.

Dallas has now taken on another role: primary carer for the woman he loves. And much like his other pursuits, he’s determined to do the best job he can.

“You have to learn as she de-learns,” he recalls being told.

Earlier this year, Dallas handed over his business, DA Transfer, where he spent years bringing treasured family memories back to life by converting old videotapes into digital recordings.

Dallas (centre), Bonnie (right) and their son Bradley bringing the cool to Christmas. Photo: Supplied.

Now, his focus is on caring for Bonnie. He’s turned to online resources for advice on making her days more comfortable and predictable, continually adapting his approach as her needs change.

“Being a husband and a carer, there’s no difference … she’s the love of my life, I care, and that’s that.”

And while Dallas has stepped away from preserving memories for other families, he’s still helping create them for hundreds of Canberra children each Christmas. Pulling on the red suit now carries extra meaning for Dallas, offering a welcome respite from his caring responsibilities.

He delights in being recognised outside the shopping centre, offering a knowing wink or a tap of his nose when a wide-eyed child tugs at their parent’s arm in disbelief.

This year, he’s requested morning shifts so he can be home with Bonnie in the afternoons, when she experiences increased confusion associated with a dementia symptom known as sundowning.

“I don’t want to give up Santa. It’s my release. It really is,” Dallas says. Photo: Supplied

Dallas knows the years ahead will bring new challenges, but he intends to be by Bonnie’s side every step of the way.

And while their life together hasn’t yet brought them grandchildren, Dallas has found a rather magical silver lining, complete with sleigh bells, sugarplums and hundreds of little faces waiting to see him each Christmas.

“When I teach my Santas, my main thing is, treat every child as your own personal grandkids. So if I never get any, I’ve got hundreds, right?”

For Dallas, the magic isn’t just in the tricks or the presents. It’s in those final moments when a child walks away, still looking back at Santa in wonder.

“If they’re looking back at you, in awe, and you’re still waving … you’ve won a heart, and they’ll be back next year for the same reason.”

Santa Dallas Atkins will be at Westfield Woden right up until Christmas. For information and to book photos for 2026, head to the Westfield Woden website.

Away from the red suit, Dallas shares another passion through his YouTube channel, Santa Poke Packs, where he explores the world of Pokémon trading cards.

canberra.title: The shape of things to come? Canberra’s stadium debate is going round in circles
canberra.snippet: Canberra sports fans are suffering from whiplash at the moment amidst the public airing of ideas surrounding the proposed new lakeside st...
canberra.content:
21 November 2026

Join the conversation

2

A concept image for a Civic stadium as proposed in 2022. Photo: GHDWoodhead.

Canberra sports fans are suffering from whiplash at the moment amidst the public airing of ideas surrounding the proposed new lakeside stadium.

Should it be 25,000 seats? Will the planned aquatic facility and the new stadium fit together on the Commonwealth Park footprint? Should it be rectangular or oval-shaped? Or should we instead focus on a super stadium at Bruce catering for AFL and cricket as well as rugby league, union and soccer? And what about a roof?

Added to the mix is the suggestion that any new stadium could be pivotal in Canberra securing an AFL licence and Big Bash franchise.

Tellingly, one of the advocates for the lakeside stadium, Cricket ACT Chairman Greg Boorer, a key force in the Big Bash bid, has seemingly rejected the push for the oval-shaped configuration on the shores of Lake Burley Griffin.

He says moving to an oval-shaped facility would affect the viability of the lakeside stadium, with cricket and AFL continuing to play at Manuka.

Complaints about the condition of Bruce Stadium are well known, but Manuka Oval needs some love, too. Photo: Thomas Lucraft.

It’s worth pointing out that Manuka needs an upgrade with increased seating, improved corporate facilities and revamped basic amenities.

In an earlier column, I pointed out how the fan experience for rectangular sporting codes is significantly diminished when played on an oval-shaped ground.

Now, with Chief Minister Andrew Barr suggesting the option of a super stadium at Bruce, with the ability to host AFL, cricket, the rugby codes and soccer, the focus has again shifted.

While attention should be on how we can get the lakeside stadium off the ground, we will spend valuable time and resources debating whether it should be oval or rectangular, and whether it should be at Bruce or on the shores of Lake Burley Griffin.

Then there is the emerging argument over parking.

At major stadiums in Australia, most patrons use public transport for at least part of the journey.

Travel by private car is the least-favoured option.

The proposed lakeside stadium is perfectly positioned to take advantage of the light rail and inner-city parking, and then a walk to the ground.

My concern is that we are heading down another rabbit hole where it all becomes too hard as conflicting ideas are thrown into the mix and nothing gets done.

Is that another feasibility study I can see being produced?

canberra.title: Party veteran says he can rev up complacent Canberra Liberals after Morris bows out of presidency
canberra.snippet: Liberal Party veteran Gerry Wheeler has thrown his hat into the ring for the ACT presidency after Adam Morris decided to step down after ...
canberra.content:
Canberra Liberals president Adam Morris – who hasn’t been renominated – with leader Mark Parton. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Liberal Party veteran Gerry Wheeler has thrown his hat into the ring for the ACT presidency after Adam Morris decided to step down after only a year in the job.

The Canberra Liberals, known in recent years for its internal divisions, holds its Annual General Meeting next Tuesday (24 November), and Mr Morris told the committee this week that he would not be renominating due to work commitments.

When he was elected president last year, he and his wife, parliamentary Deputy Leader Deborah Morris, were touted as the party’s right-wing power couple. However, some questioned whether they should hold these offices at the same time.

In the party’s weekly update, Mr Morris urged members to leave the past division behind.

“We cannot afford a return to division and disunity which will only lead to electoral failure,” he said.

Mr Wheeler is pushing hard for the top job, saying in a letter to members that he was alarmed by the lack of preparation for the 2028 federal and ACT elections and the failure to implement the Hannam review’s recommendations, which he links to the 2024 ACT defeat.

Mr Wheeler is a former party federal vice-president, adviser to former prime minister John Howard, and policy director for former Opposition Leader Sussan Ley.

He is a strong supporter of Senate candidate Nick Tyrrell, himself a former ACT president. He has put together a ticket with Chris Faulks, a former CEO of the Canberra Business Chamber, and party elder Gary Humphries, a former ACT senator and chief minister.

It is understood Mr Tyrrell is unhappy so far with the extent of party support for his campaign.

Mr Wheeler wasn’t intending to nominate but “I can’t watch us walk into two elections unprepared when I know how to fix it”.

“As President, I will chair the campaign committee myself, and my job will be to get this Division match-fit to win,” he told members.

Mr Wheeler said to win the federal election, due before the October ACT election, the party must build the volunteers, donors, data and momentum currently missing.

“A victory for Nick will give us momentum to carry into the 2028 Assembly campaign, only months later, when we must win additional Liberal seats. One campaign machine to win two elections,” he said.

Mr Wheeler has promised in his first 30 days as president to revive the ACT Division’s campaign committee, recruit a Divisional Director, left vacant after the departure of Adam Wojtonis on unexplained leave, and implement the recommendations of the Hannan review where possible.

Mr Wheeler is up against Robert Gunning, while Ms Faulks is taking on Louise Rostron.

Mr Humphries has nominated for Policy Committee Chair, against Joshua Osborne-Goldsbrough.

Other nominations are Peter Peppas and Michael Keating for Finance Committee Chair; James Daniels as Honorary Treasurer; Supre Ponnappa, Megan Fox, Jessica Wright, Josh Cronin, Hugh Miller, Peter Peppas and Michael Keating for the four-person Policy Committee; and Adam Wojtonis and Arthur Potter as Federal Regional and Rural Committee Representative.

australia.title: Teenager allegedly organised arsons and kidnapping on Signal during Melbourne hospitality wars
australia.snippet: Victoria police say boy, 17, communicated with offenders under username ‘Onepercent’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news...
australia.content:
Victorian police allege a 17-year-old boy tasked others to carry out a series of arsons, home invasions and a mistaken identity kidnapping that resulted in the partial amputation of a victim’s finger during Melbourne’s hospitality wars.

The boy, who was arrested on Friday afternoon, allegedly communicated with the offenders under the username “Onepercent” on the encrypted communications app Signal.

He was charged on Saturday with extortion, making threats to kill, three offences of criminal damage by fire, and home invasion. He was remanded to appear in court later on Saturday.

In a statement, police said it would be alleged that Onepercent was involved in tasking an arson at a York Street, South Melbourne licensed premises on 15 April; two home invasions and a kidnapping four days apart in Springvale later that month; and two arson attacks during March at a Williamstown ice-cream store and a car in Moonee Ponds.

The boy was arrested at a house in the Moonee Ponds region, in Melbourne’s north-west, police said.

It is alleged a trafficable quantity of cocaine, three phones and cash were seized during the arrest.

Police allege that when the mistaken identity kidnapping occurred at the Springvale property on 22 April, a 34-year-old victim received serious injuries to his lower body and the partial amputation of one of his fingers.

It is alleged the fire at Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown on 22 March caused $600,000 worth of damage and endangered the lives of residents at the property upstairs.

On 16 November, police appealed for more information about the person behind the Onepercent user name.

“We need the public’s assistance to identify the user of this handle,” Det Insp Graham Banks said at the time.

“There will be people in the wider organised crime network and in our community who will have intimate knowledge of who this person is.

“We are hopeful that those people may now be in a position to come forward and speak to police.”

australia.title: Victorian Greens seek urgent injunction over how-to-vote cards mimicking party’s branding but preferencing it last
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s cards instruct people to vote in a way that would benefit Liberal party Get our dai...
australia.content:
The Victorian Greens are seeking an urgent injunction from the supreme court to stop an independent candidate distributing how-to-vote cards that allegedly mimic the party’s branding and urge people to preference it last.

As prepoll opened on Wednesday morning, Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign team handed out how-to-vote cards that used the minor party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo with the banner “Vote 1 Green Values”.

The card instructed people to vote in a way that would ultimately benefit the Liberal party. It asked voters to give their first preference to Finnigan followed by an Animal Justice party candidate, another independent candidate and then the Liberals in fourth place.

The Greens are determined to win back the ultra-marginal seat it lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection with a 1.3% margin. Labor is running an open ticket in Prahran, which the Greens fear could deprive it of the preference votes it needs.

On Wednesday afternoon, the Greens state director, Martin Shield, requested Finnigan immediately stop distributing the material and threatened to take legal action if an undertaking was not given to do so in less than two hours.

Finnigan agreed to the request and produced an amended how-to-vote card within hours that included different colours with a revised banner that said “Vote 1 Trans Greens Values”.

“Due to legal threats from the Greens party, I confirm that I am not an endorsed Greens party candidate,” a disclaimer on Finnigan’s revised how-to-vote card said.

But the changes did not satisfy the Greens. On Friday afternoon, the party’s lawyers lodged papers in the supreme court.

At an initial hearing on Friday night, the Greens’ lawyer, Adam McBeth, alleged people handing out Finnigan’s material at prepoll wore shirts with the exact shade of green as worn by genuine Greens party volunteers.

McBeth alleged Finnigan’s team stood next to Greens party volunteers and Greens placards. The party argues voters at prepoll were deliberately misled.

“There is no other reason for an independent candidate who has an infinite range of colours and styles to choose from to so closely mimic the Greens, including the way people paid to hand out were dressed and where they were directed to stand,” McBeth said.

Finnigan, who was self-represented, said they had gone above and beyond to quickly make changes to their initial how-to-vote card and accused the Greens of using “legal manoeuvres” to stop them campaigning.

“It is my belief that they don’t want me to hand out on Saturday, which will be one of the busiest days of prepoll,” Finnigan said.

Finnigan told the court that they did not have enough money to print new cards. They said their campaign team had not been instructed to stand next to the Greens at prepoll.

“I am someone who holds Greens values, of course I am going to have some kind of green shirt,” Finnigan said.

“The honest reason I went for that colour of green is because the colour is called Irish green and I am of Irish background. That’s why I went for it. I just like the sound of Irish green.”

On Friday evening, after the supreme court action was lodged, the Victorian Election Commission (VEC) accepted Finnigan’s subsequent how-to-vote card and published it online.

Justice John Watson said the first how-to-vote card “looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate”, but he adjourned the matter until 3pm on Saturday to hear testimony from the VEC.

A decision on whether to grant an injunction will be made on Sunday morning.

Finnigan became Victoria’s first openly transgender councillor in 2023 when they were elected to the Colac Otway shire council after a countback. They resigned from the council in October 2024.

The former Labor field campaigner founded the Restore Democracy Sack Dan Andrews party in 2022. They unsuccessfully contested an upper house seat for the party, securing 1% of first preference votes.

After working in the offices of Labor ministers during the 2014 state campaign, Finnigan became a whistleblower in the so-called Red Shirts scandal, which saw taxpayer funds used to pay electorate officers campaigning for Labor.

Finnigan’s campaign Facebook page carrying an authorisation message describes them as a “Green Independent” and contains attack ads against the minor party.

australia.title: NSW passes Mount Pleasant coalmine law as Greens claim change an attempt to head off One Nation
australia.snippet: Labor says allowing mine to increase production reflects ‘gravity of situation facing hundreds of workers’ – but critics call it ‘unprece...
australia.content:
The New South Wales government has passed special legislation to allow a coalmine in the Hunter Valley to increase production by 32% in its final act of parliament before the March state election, in which the region will be a key battleground for One Nation.

After a marathon session in the legislative council on Friday, the Minns government and the Coalition voted at 1.36am on Saturday morning to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to increase its annual extraction rate from 12.5MT to 16.5MT until 2032.

At the start of debate, the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, told the upper house “this is a unique bill applying to unique circumstances”.

“Taking the decision to intervene in the way we have is not an easy one, but it is an important one,” she said. “And it does reflect the gravity of the situation facing hundreds of workers and their families in the Hunter.”

The legislation has drawn outcry from legal and anti-corruption experts, climate groups, crossbenchers and civil liberties organisations, after the high court ruled last month that an approval for an expansion that would increase the mine’s annual output to 21MT until 2048 was invalid.

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to properly consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burned overseas.

Despite saying he would not bypass the court’s decision, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, subsequently announced the legislation, claiming it would save 400 jobs ahead of Christmas. Minns has rejected the idea the legislation goes around the high court decision.

On Friday, the government and Coalition used their numbers to block almost 200 amendments to the bill sought by the Greens, who called the legislation “exceptional and unprecedented and dangerous”. Animal Justice party MLC Emma Hurst also opposed the bill.

“Labor describes the circumstances as exceptional, says this case is unique, and assures the public that other companies shouldn’t expect the same treatment,” the Greens climate spokesperson, Sue Higginson, told the parliament.

“But a political assurance offers no protection against the precedent being set.”

She accused the premier of being motivated by a desire to withstand a threat from One Nation to Labor seats in the Hunter.

“It’s very clear to us why Chris Minns has gone here, and that is because we’re really on the eve of an election, and One Nation is right now his threat,” she said at a press conference on Thursday.

The Hunter region, the centre of NSW’s coalmining industry, is emerging as a key battleground at the March 2027 state election. The One Nation NSW upper house candidate and former coalminer Stuart Bonds contested the Labor-held federal seat of Hunter in 2025, winning 41% of the two-candidate preferred vote. The party’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, is running in the Labor-held lower house seat of Cessnock.

Higginson told the upper house that in bringing the bill, the government had turned its back on the advice of the state’s Net Zero Commission, which has said further coalmine expansions are incompatible with meeting legislated emissions reduction targets.

“But who seems to care any more? What does the rule of law matter when [the premier] visits the Hunter and decides he needs to do something for someone so that he can remain somewhat popular in his own mind?” she said.

The Coalition, which supported the bill, said it was “about people”.

“It’s about the hundreds of workers at MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant mine who, since the high court handed down its decision in October, have been left wondering whether they will still have a job in the new year,” Nationals MLC Sarah Mitchell said.

She said “losing hundreds of jobs in one go would completely devastate the Hunter region”.

The legislation ties consent for the mine expansion to a jobs guarantee protecting workers at the mine. Data provided to the government by the mine for the jobs guarantee, which covers more than 720 workers, is subject to an independent audit.

At a press conference on Wednesday, Minns said the legal proceedings would return to the land and environment court for consideration, but it would be “a tragedy if, in the meantime, that community effectively shut down as a result of this decision”.

“Most of the workers from Mount Pleasant live in Muswellbrook, and if the mine closed, the unemployment rate would jump by 5% just in that small town,” he said, speaking alongside workers at the mine and the Mining and Energy Union, which has welcomed the legislation.

‘Serious corruption risk’

In a report published on Tuesday, the parliament’s legislation review committee found the Mount Pleasant bill would “effectively undermine” proceedings that were still before the land and environment court and “would undermine procedural fairness” by removing avenues for legal challenge.

That report also highlighted concerns with a so-called Henry VIII clause that the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson warned this week posed a “serious corruption risk” to the state.

The clause, allowing the resources minister of the day to override state laws as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development, was amended by the government in the lower house. Following the amendments, it cannot be used to prevent development from being subject to Icac investigations or to change the permitted coal production limit.

The Nature Conservation Council of NSW said the government had been “embarrassed into amending its own coalmining bill”, while the Greens said the amendments did not go far enough to constrain the power any resources minister might hold under the clause.

The Law Society of NSW said on Thursday it was concerned that without further amendments, the Henry VIII clause risked “undermining the rule of law”.

Houssos told the upper house on Friday the government had carefully considered concerns and moved amendments to the clause because it “recognises the importance of appropriate safeguards and accountability”.

australia.title: Angela’s home birth could be upended by Australia’s new insurance rules. Midwives fear it will drive women to freebirths
australia.snippet: Expiry of longstanding insurance exemption for midwives on 31 December threatens to throw private home birth sector into collapse Sign up...
australia.content:
Sydney mother Angela Morata is four months’ pregnant with her third child. The 35-year-old is due in April next year and, just as she did with her other two babies, has scheduled a home birth.

“I booked my midwife the day I took the pregnancy test,” she says. “I know how amazing the experience can be at home, and I wouldn’t want it to be any different.”

But the expiry of a longstanding insurance exemption for midwives on 31 December threatens to upend her plans.

From 1 January, all privately practising midwives attending home births must be covered by a government insurance policy. The scheme will be available exclusively to “endorsed midwives”, an accreditation that requires additional study and training, including 5,000 clinical hours.

Endorsed midwives are allowed to prescribe medicines and write referrals for blood tests, ultrasounds and other tests. According to the Nursing and Midwifery Board of Australia, about 5% of almost 35,000 registered midwives are endorsed.

Health experts warn the change could collapse the private home birth sector and leave those expecting, like Morata, scrambling for alternative birthing options.

Morata says it would “break my heart” if her home birth plans fell through.

‘The burnout would be huge’

In Australia, two midwives are legally required at every home birth: a “primary” midwife, who is endorsed and leads the care, and a supporting second midwife who in many cases is not endorsed.

The Australian College of Midwives warns that up to a third of privately practising endorsed midwives, particularly those who rely on non-endorsed colleagues as second attendants, could be forced out of the system when changes take effect.

Sydney-based endorsed midwife Jo Hunter says the changes “could mean having to cease practice”.

She relies on a network of other private midwives who support each other’s businesses, all of whom could be affected because “they all rely on non-endorsed midwives as second attendants at births”.

She says relying on other endorsed midwives is an “unsustainable” business model.

“That then means you’re doing double the work because you’d have to go to each other’s births,” she says. “I take on four births a month … if I’m having to attend eight because I’m supporting my colleague and she’s supporting me, the burnout would be huge. You’d never sleep, for a start. It’s unsustainable.”

Hunter is booked out until July next year. As the deadline approaches, she says she is increasingly receiving “text messages and phone calls saying, ‘Am I going to be able to still have my home birth?’

“When that woman has been planning for her birth and paid for it to be in her home, and all of a sudden the rug is pulled out from underneath her … it’s really, really concerning,” she says.

‘Entering into the perfect storm’

Western Sydney University professor Hannah Dahlen, the director of research in the School of Nursing and Midwifery, says there is strong evidence that a mass exodus of private midwives could see freebirths skyrocket and create a “potentially very risky situation for the public”.

A freebirth is a birth outside hospital without medical assistance, often supported by family, friends, a doula or a “birth keeper”. In recent years, a number of high-profile deaths have been linked to the practice, with coronial inquests in New South Wales and Victoria examining the role of freebirths in deaths.

“We know from 20 years of research that one of the reasons women choose to freebirth is that they can’t access a midwife, or they can’t afford to pay for one. And both those issues are going to become worse, particularly in rural and regional Australia,” Dahlen says.

She says women who choose to give birth at home “often have a particular philosophical paradigm that they want honoured and respected” and they “won’t just meekly walk into a hospital” if being supported by midwives is no longer an option.

“Our hospital system has one of the highest intervention rates. More and more women are seeking an alternative because they are not happy with what they’re being provided with in hospital,” she says.

“We are literally entering into the perfect storm here, which is restricting that access more and expanding the very thing that we’re all very worried about, which is women birthing with no health professional in attendance.”

The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists declined to comment when asked about whether they share this concern.

Katelyn Commerford, coordinator and NSW president of Homebirth Australia, says pregnant women tell her they feel “left between a rock and a hard place”.

“They are saying in no uncertain terms that they will continue to birth at home … they just won’t have access to their midwives at home. That opens the floodgates to a whole other public health concern.”

Homebirth Australia has called on the government to grant midwives another extension and find a permanent solution by the 31 December deadline.

“We’ve made it really clear to the government that we will hold them accountable for any outcomes of women feeling forced to freebirth,” Commerford says. “That will absolutely be the government’s responsibility and burden to bear.”

In a statement to Guardian Australia, the federal health department said midwives attending home births had previously been exempt because “there was not a suitable insurance product available”, and that the exemption “was never intended to be a permanent solution to address the issue of appropriate insurance”.

The department acknowledged concerns about access to home birth services, particularly in rural and regional communities, but said the policy change was not intended “to discourage women from choosing a home birth” but rather “to support safe and appropriate maternity care”.

In the meantime, Morata who is also a midwife, says she will “nervously” await developments ahead of her due date.

“As women, different things in our life are already taken control of in different ways and already treated with not as much respect as it should be. And birth and motherhood is one of those things,” she says.

“It’s really horrible that people like me may not get that chance because of something that’s misunderstood.”

australia.title: ‘We don’t talk about the God stuff’: a day with Padre Dave, the outback’s flying minister
australia.snippet: David Shrimpton has helped draft cattle and dehorn bulls in his decades visiting remote properties. Religion rarely gets a mention The pl...
australia.content:
The plane rattles as it bounces in the wind. Olive vinyl and carpet line the doors and floor, and a faded sticker on the dashboard reads: “Smoking is permitted.”

At the yoke of the 1970s Cessna, smiling through a white moustache and glasses, sits a man in a suit and tie patterned with cartoon aeroplanes. Padre Dave is on his way to marry two old friends.

David Shrimpton, 62, has dedicated his life to serving his faith. He was part of the Baptist church growing up in Geelong and became a minister alongside his wife, Jennie.

For more than two decades he has flown across some of the most remote parts of Australia. From his base in Broken Hill, in outback western New South Wales, he covers about 200,000 sq km – roughly the size of England and Scotland combined – performing weddings, funerals and baptisms, or simply dropping in for a cuppa.

“It’s basically a chaplaincy role for those in the bush,” he says. “Flying is just an easy way of getting to those places.”

Shrimpton started flying lessons in Port Pirie in the late 1990s. When the Salvation Army heard, they offered to pay for his pilot’s licence on the condition he’d end up in Darwin to take up their flying padre chaplaincy, a role that has been offering pastoral support across a vast outback constituency since 1945.

“I thought, ‘What would I want to go to Darwin for? I’m happy here.’ And they said, ‘Well, we’ve got a plane up there.’”

The Shrimptons moved north in 2003 and spent the next 11 years flying across the Northern Territory and Western Australia. They flew to huge outback stations and remote communities, “ringing up, landing at a station, catching up with the manager, the head stockmen, the cook – whoever is around at the time, and just having a chat”.

“As someone who has no connection to the running of things, I’m a safe person who they can talk to about pretty well anything and they know it’s not going to get back to anyone,” Shrimpton says.

  • Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

In 2014 the couple moved to Broken Hill to take up another flying chaplaincy role, this time with the Uniting church.

“It’s all by design,” Shrimpton says as he looks from the window down on the ephemeral outback lakes, full after a year of rain in the region. “Nothing to do with my doing, apart from saying yes, and giving things a go.”

Flying padres have existed in Australia for more than a century, starting with the Rev Leonard Daniels in 1928, who serviced the NSW far west for the Uniting church from a base at Wilcannia. That inspired the Rev John Flynn, who launched the Royal Flying Doctor Service in the same year.

Shrimpton says he barely talks about religion in his day-to-day work.

“We don’t talk about the God stuff,” he says. “It’s about the personal stuff, about where people are at.”

Chaplaincy for people living remotely mostly involves listening, he says.

“You’re going into their territory, so you can’t tell them, ‘Hey, watch your language.’ You’ve got to accept them for who they are, they’ll call a spade a spade.”

On a busy station there isn’t always time to sit down to talk over a cup of tea, so Shrimpton gets put to work. He has helped draft cattle and dehorn bulls, and sometimes just jumps in a ute and tags along.

“You ask, ‘Is there anything I can do?’ And you make yourself useful.”

Adele Cullinan, who lives on a station in the southern half of Shrimpton’s range, says she chose to baptise her daughters because of his influence. “Because of how he practises his religion,” she says. “He doesn’t preach, he’s just a friend.”

Cullinan says her kids can spot his plane coming before she can. “They get so excited to see Padre’s plane. All the kids know his plane compared to any other.”

Back in the cockpit, Shrimpton pushes the yoke as the plane begins another descent, still being bounced around by the wind outside. He points to an arbour that has been installed on the side of a lake.

“That’s where we’re going,” he says. “Looks like they’ve started setting up.”

A humble red-dirt runway appears amid the desert scrub and Shrimpton touches down.

Alongside the runway, a wedding guest, Brett, jumps out of his ute to greet us. Shrimpton officiated at his wedding to his wife, Sammy, on their family farm in 2022.

Brett loads Shrimpton into his ute and drives to Bancannia Lake, the lake we spotted from the sky, where a group of men stand in suits, beers in hand.

One of them, who today will marry his partner, Trudy.

The couple met while working at nearby Nundooka station, and Ben had just one condition for their wedding: “We’ll get married when the lake fills up.”

This year, it did.

“We had a fair bit of pressure,” Trudy says, laughing. “A lot of neighbours rang up and were like, ‘You know the lake’s full, don’t you?’”

The pair are eloping by the side of the lake and it’s a do-it-yourself kind of affair.

Shrimpton immediately jumps in to help set up, moving tables, helping to add flowers to the arbour and showing the groomsmen how to pin their boutonnieres.

The small group stand in the red dirt by the arbour, the afternoon sun reflecting off the water behind them.

After the ceremony Shrimpton jumps back into the plane – he has another event to attend today.

There are plenty more people to visit. Sometimes for a specific reason but not always. “Physically calling in to say g’day, it’s not a normal thing to do any more,” he says.

“I still love flying but it’s not the flying that keeps me doing it. It’s meeting people. And they’re happy to have you.”

The Cessna lifts into the wind. Below, the lake holds its water.

world.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
world.snippet: Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded Multiple coastal hazard warnings we...
world.content:
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

After a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

world.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
world.snippet: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Afri...
world.content:
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.

The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.

“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.

Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.

“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”

Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”

Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.

The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.

A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

world.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
world.snippet: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around ...
world.content:
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.

Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”

She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.

“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

world.title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
world.snippet: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose ...
world.content:
Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.

The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.

Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”

In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”

He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.

It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.

The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.

The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.

Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

world.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
world.snippet: Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans The European Commission has been a...
world.content:
The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”

Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.

The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.

One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.

In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.

The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.

During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.

She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”

Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.

It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.

Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.
